newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai soymeal imports pick up as prices drop.
newsitem.headline: Thai soymeal imports pick up as prices drop.

text.p: The Thai grain market was livelier this week because of lower prices and the animal feed industry importing more soymeal, trade sources said on Tuesday.
Domestic corn prices also eased because farmers sold more supplies to the market before the scheduled debt repayments to the state-run agriculture bank later this month.
Trade sources said they heard some feed producers bought a total of "a cargo or two" of soymeal for December and January shipments.

One trader told Reuters that his trading house received 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes of buying orders for Indian-origin soymeal for December 15 to January 15 shipment. The price was quoted at around $304 cost and freight (c&f) Bangkok.
"I would expect more buying if the prices fall further," said one trader.
But other traders disagreed, saying short-term buying would be limited because more soymeal from oil crushers would be available in the market soon.
About 100,000 tonnes of U.S. soybean, imported by vegetable oil producers, was expected to arrive at Thai ports between late December and early January, trade and shipping sources said.
The vessel Yick Kam had left the Gulf of Mexico with 47,000 tonnes of soybean and was expected to arrive on December 5, they said.
Vessel Avalanche was scheduled to load 50,000 tonnes of soybean between November 28 and December 5 and was likely to arrive by the end of December or early January.
The soymeal price was quoted at around 9.20 baht a kg ($0.36) this week from 9.20-9.50 baht a kg a week earlier.
Meanwhile, corn prices dropped slightly to 4.20-4.30 baht a kg from 4.28-4.40 baht a kg last week.
Some traders said prices could rise after the Thai Maize and Produce Traders Association released its 1996/97 (July-June) revised its output forecast on Wednesday.
They said the forecast was rumoured to be lower than expected.
"The figure is being reviewed. But I heard it is likely to be below four million tonnes," one trader said.

The agriculture ministry's latest forecast put 1996/97 corn output at 4.38 million tonnes, saying that flood damage during the June-October monsoon season was offset by higher yields from a new corn hybrid.
